When this subverse first started up, I mentioned that I have spiderworts all over my yard, which have been growing wild since we moved in over a decade ago (meaning we never planted them - we maintain our lawn).

All of the spiderwort flowers have always been a deep purple color, every year without fail. That is - until 2011. That spring, one of our spiderworts bloomed pink instead of purple. It has bloomed pink every year since then. 2011 was the year of the Fukushima Daiichi disaster. I've read that spiderworts can serve as radiation detectors in the environment, and they do so by changing their bloom color. (See: [Spiderworts via GDR.org] http://www.gdr.org/spiderwortdefon.htm))

Iâ€™m not about to undergo expensive testing that would be necessary to detect if this particular plant was actually exposed to radiation. Not to mention the fact that I am not about to bring the attention of any authorities to my home (which, knowing my luck, my house would be condemned and I would have bureaucratic hell rain down on me). I thought you all might find it interesting, though.

This is a pic of the flowers side by side, purple on the left, pink on the right. Sorry the pink is so washed out. It's a really sunny day and you have to photograph them in the morning hours before they close up for the night. This plant happens to be on the east side of the property (where the sun was most intense at that hour). https://sli.mg/X7PUTY

Possible and interesting hypothesis. Unless you live on the West Coast, I do find it doubtful (even then, odds are against)... but it's definitely interesting. I suspect a more mundane cause is the culprit. For instance, hydrangeas are known to change bloom color based on soil pH.

Would you happen to have another link for the spiderwort/radiation hypothesis? You've got me curious myself.

I frankly don't think this is directly tied to Fukushima, especially because I am on the far east coast. 12 miles from the Atlantic, in fact. The timing was the interesting coincidence. The flowers bloom in March and that is when Fukushima happened. The pink one is among other spiderwort plants in the same area of the lawn and they are all still purple (blue, technically correct).

Not sure how in depth you want to get on the radiation speculation. Easy read at Wiki: Tradescantia, a little more in depth with this Comparative Study from the Chicago Botanical Garden: PDF: A Comparative Study of Tradescantia Cultivars, and publication way over my head from Kyoto University: Somatic Mutation Rate In Tradescantia Stamen Hairs At Low Radiation Levels: Finding Of Low Doubling Doses Of Mutations.

Truly a curiosity, but not much more.
I don't think you have anything to worry about, like antiplebbitor said. You could see if you can get your hands on a giger counter or make one of you really want to feel secure.
